detail: policyengine.py 6.16.1 (policyengine-uk 2.174.1, bundle uk-6.16.1) on its certified Microcosm UK 2024-25 national dataset, release microcosm-uk-2024-25-national-20261107T020434Z-eeb6093e, loaded through the package's managed loader and checked against the bundle's SHA-256.

Each household's annual electricity and gas use in kWh comes from the dataset's export (calendar 2024: gas levelled to DESNZ Energy Trends domestic volumes, electricity to ONS 2024 spending) and is held fixed. The dataset's spending columns are those kWh priced at DESNZ Quarterly Energy Prices CY2024 (regional unit cost plus fixed cost, 5% VAT included); the pipeline checks that basis but costs every scenario from kWh. 3.6% of households use no electricity and pay only the standing charge; 15.9% have no mains gas and pay no gas standing charge.

Central estimate uses Ofgem's winter shares: 75% of gas and 57% of electricity used in October–March, split equally between the two quarters of each half-year; standing charges are time-weighted. Equal quarterly use is reported as a sensitivity (2026-27: typical bill £1,995.83 seasonal vs £1,923.34 equal-weight, extra cost £8.48bn vs £6.82bn; 2027-28: typical bill £2,158.64 seasonal vs £2,174.31 equal-weight, extra cost £12.74bn vs £13.1bn).

Ofgem cut typical consumption on 1 Jul 2026, so published caps from July (£1,663, £1,723, £1,999) can't be compared with £1,641. Every quarter is re-costed from unit rates and standing charges at the old 2,700 / 11,500 kWh.

Post-Budget law at forecast prices: the Household Energy Payment and the electricity VAT extension announced in Budget 2026 are in the baseline. Each household's kWh are costed at each quarter's tariffs and the resulting electricity and gas bills are loaded into PolicyEngine. The Energy Price Guarantee ended in April 2024, so it pays nothing.

Their effect is measured against a counterfactual with the same prices, data and other policies but no Household Energy Payment and electricity VAT as under SI 2026/987 alone. The payment reaches 19.6m households in 2026-27 at £1.96bn; the VAT extension saves households £0.36bn in 2027-28.

£100 to households in council tax bands A–D in England in 2026-27, paid by local authorities from January 2027. policyengine-uk pays every household in those bands (it cannot identify landlords liable for council tax) and counts the payment in household and HBAI income, as DWP counted the 2022 Council Tax Rebate, so it moves poverty. The devolved governments' Barnett share is not allocated.

Every household is modelled on the capped variable tariff. Around 35% of households are on fixed tariffs and will not see the October 2026 cap rise (Ofgem); tariff type, payment method and contract expiry are not modelled, and no correction is inferred from the 35% share. The electricity VAT cut reaches fixed-tariff customers too.

VAT on domestic electricity is 0% in England, Wales and Scotland from 1 Oct 2026 (SI 2026/987). Budget 2026 extends the zero rate to 30 June 2027 and expects it to apply in Northern Ireland from 1 April 2027; this is announced policy, not yet law. The rate is 5% from 1 July 2027. Each quarter's published electricity rates are taken back to their VAT-exclusive level and priced at the rate in force for that quarter and nation, so the April–June 2027 supplier forecast, made at 5%, is reduced. policyengine-uk's own energy VAT (a fiscal-year day-weighted rate on bills ÷ 1.05) is not used: no simulation changes a VAT rate, so it never reaches income and VAT savings are counted once.

April–September 2027 use the average of supplier forecasts (EDF, British Gas, E.ON Next); October–December 2027 uses OVO's forecast, and January–March 2028 holds that level. Forecasts give no fuel split, so Cornwall Insight's January 2027 rates as forecast on 30 Sep 2026 are scaled to each total. These forecasts predate the Budget and are unchanged.

Electricity and gas unit rates and standing charges are held at April–June 2026 levels. The cost is each household's forecast bill minus its bill at those tariffs for the same kWh, floored at zero. It is a price restoration, so it sits outside HBAI income and has no poverty effect.

Keeps 0% VAT on domestic electricity from 1 July 2027 to 31 March 2028, UK-wide like the Budget's extension. Its cost is the additional relief beyond the extension to June 2027, which is already in the baseline.

A simplified fixed-payment illustration of the Resolution Foundation's unit-rate discount, with three assumptions: a flat £175 per eligible household (RF's average) rather than a unit-rate discount; an annual income test rather than the previous three months' income; and full take-up. Eligible: GB households on means-tested benefits or whose highest individual income is under £24,000.

An extra £100 on the Warm Home Discount rebate, paid from taxation (the £150 rebate itself stays funded by suppliers through bills and is in the baseline's HBAI income through policyengine-uk). Eligibility follows the scheme: in England and Wales, households where anyone receives Pension Credit, Universal Credit, Housing Benefit or income-related ESA (the eligibility statement for 2026-27, read from policyengine-uk); in Scotland, the core group that receives the rebate without applying (Pension Credit; Universal Credit with a disability or health element; income-related ESA with a disability premium; a child under 5 with Universal Credit and no earnings, or income-related ESA). Scotland's broader group applies to suppliers under supplier-set criteria and is shown only as a sensitivity. Receipt follows DESNZ's rates (85% of Pension Credit households, 70% of others; impact assessment para. 40, with Table 8 applying them to Scotland) through policyengine-uk's own seeded draw, so in England and Wales the top-up reaches the same households as the model's £150 rebate. Timing: paid with the rebate, by 31 March of the scheme year (qualifying date 23 August 2026 for 2026-27); the model uses benefit receipt over the year, not on the qualifying date. 2026-27: 7.3m eligible, 5.2m receive it, £0.52bn; 2027-28: 7.3m eligible, 5.2m receive it, £0.52bn. Sensitivities in options.json: full receipt, the impact assessment's 60% and 80% other-benefits rates, England and Wales only, Scotland's broader group, and DESNZ's estimate of around 6 million recipient households in winter 2025/26 (Government Response, January 2026, p. 5).

Relative poverty: people in households below 60% of median equivalised HBAI income (PolicyEngine UK in_relative_poverty_bhc/ahc, the DWP headline measure). Absolute poverty (in_poverty_*, a fixed FYE 2025 line) is also exported. Child rates (child_*) are under-18 rates (age < 18), not DWP's dependent-child cohort, which includes some 16-19-year-olds in full-time non-advanced education. HBAI income counts the Household Energy Payment, the Warm Home Discount and (as DWP did for the 2022 Energy Bills Support Scheme) the £400 credit, so they move poverty; the RF discount is counted the same way by assumption. Price cuts (VAT, cap freeze, levies) lower bills rather than raise income, so they do not move HBAI poverty.

Deciles of equivalised HBAI household income before housing costs, person-weighted (household weight × household size), as PolicyEngine UK defines household_income_decile. As in HBAI, negative incomes are reset to zero and ranked in the bottom decile. Gains shown are household-weighted means within each decile.

Households with more than one benefit unit (for example adult children or sharers) are grouped as 'Multiple family units'; other households take their family type, split by whether anyone is over State Pension age.
A static scenario: households keep the same kWh, and benefit uprating does not respond to higher inflation. Northern Ireland uses GB prices as a proxy.

Autumn Budget 2026 and the OBR's forecast were published on 28 October 2026. The energy price forecasts used here were made before the Budget and are unchanged; Ofgem's January–March 2027 cap can replace Cornwall Insight's forecast separately.
